Frequently Asked Questions
How often is the report be released?
The report is released monthly.
Is EIA saying that the rig count is no longer relevant
No.  The rig count remains one of the crucial indicators of oil and natural gas  production changes. It is just not the entire story. The Drilling Productivity  Report (DPR) shows how the rig count, the efficiency or speed of drilling an  average well, the expected oil and natural gas yield from newly drilled wells,  and the change in production from legacy wells all interact to determine regional  production levels.
What does the DPR rig count represent?
The rig count for each region is the monthly average number of rigs operating in the region over the course of the specified month. It is derived from the Baker Hughes Inc. weekly rig count publication.
Which numbers in the report are actual data, and which numbers are projections or estimates?
The figures for rig productivity and the change in production from legacy wells are estimated trends based on the latest available data. The underlying data are often quite volatile, reflecting large variability in the performance of individual wells. The final point of actual production data as reported by the states varies, as each state has different reporting requirements and schedules. Rig count data are actual counts through the month preceding the report-release month.
Spreadsheet dates are the first day of the month. Should this be understood as the last day of the prior month, or the last day of the current month?
This date represents the average daily rate for the listed month.
Are natural gas liquids (NGL) included under oil or under natural gas? What about lease condensate and vented or flared natural gas?
The DPR uses well-level data from state reports. These reports measure hydrocarbon liquids produced at the well as oil measured in barrels and hydrocarbon gases produced at the well as natural gas measured in thousands of cubic feet. Because the DPR uses the well-level data, any separating/processing/refining occurring downstream of the well meter is not accounted for in the DPR. Lease condensate is liquid, counted in the oil stream. Natural gas production includes volumes that after being produced may be vented, flared, reinjected, separated, or otherwise processed; this is also known as produced natural gas or gross withdrawals.
Where are the aggregated U.S. total data listed?
This report purposely avoids aggregating data to the total U.S. level because one of the most important takeaways is to understand the variability of these metrics depending on where in the United States a rig is deployed.  Also, the DPR does not include all hydrocarbon producing areas.
Can you provide the raw data used to calculate the estimates and averages provided?
In some cases, the raw data used come from third- party data vendors, and EIA's contracts with these companies restrict the ability to publish raw data, allowing only aggregations of the data to be published.
Does the DPR only report shale gas/tight oil figures?
The DPR looks at total production coming from the regions indicated by county boundaries in the map provided. As such, it does not distinguish between volumes produced from shale/tight resources and those sourced from traditional hydrocarbon reservoirs. EIA has chosen the regions included in the DPR based on their recent drilling activity and rapid production increases.  Most of the drilling activity and production growth over the past couple of years has occurred in regions where shale gas and tight oil resources are being accessed.
How do metrics in other plays compare to the shale/tight plays the DPR is currently highlighting?
EIA has not targeted plays without significant shale/tight resources in the DPR analysis.  Such plays do not currently display a high degree of drilling activity or rapid production growth.
What about drilling activity in smaller, emerging plays?
The DPR focuses on the regions that are most commercially prominent at present. EIA is tracking a number of the emerging regions, and may expand the coverage of the DPR as these become increasingly important.
Why don't Bakken and Eagle Ford production figures in the DPR match the figures published by North Dakota and the Texas Railroad Commission?
In the case of the Bakken, EIA's definition of the region extends into Montana. As such, it is expected to differ from North Dakota's published Bakken data. EIA's Eagle Ford production numbers include all oil and natural gas production data available from Texas within the group of counties defined on the DPR map. The Texas Railroad Commission may have a different method of aggregating Eagle Ford production.
How did EIA determine the regional boundaries?
EIA's analysts defined shale gas and tight oil plays based on their own extensive research. The DPR regional boundaries were selected by grouping together all of the counties that reported production from those plays. The DPR model analyzes all drilling and production activity within those boundaries.
Why don't the total DPR production levels or growth rates match those of EIA's other published U.S. oil and natural gas statistics?
The DPR includes only oil and gross natural gas production found within the regions specified in the report. It does not account for the rest of the onshore production in the Lower 48 states, the Gulf of Mexico, or Alaska.
Does the DPR address the completion rate of wells in each play, which is the most critical factor in accessing new production coming onstream?
Well completion data are crucial, yet not readily accessible.  As such, EIA uses an estimated lag time from drilling activity to new-well production.  EIA has observed a high correlation between rig counts and new-well counts with a two month lag.  In some cases, where either data or industry reports suggest otherwise, a different lag may be used.
How should the legacy decline rates be interpreted? How can they be translated into well-decline curves or decline rates?
The legacy production change is the change in total regional production from one month to the next, excluding production coming from newly drilled wells. Production from a well typically declines over time, as pressure from the formation around the wellbore is depleted. In the absence of new wells being drilled, the group of all existing wells in a region will decline in production from one month to the next. As such, the DPR separates the wells in a region into groups of newly drilled wells and existing, or legacy, wells, measuring the production levels separately.  Each month, the group of newly drilled wells from the prior month is moved into the group of legacy wells, and a new group of newly drilled wells is measured. It is important to note that as the number of wells moving into the legacy group increases, the legacy production change tends to become more negative; i.e., greater total production declines from month to month. This method does not translate directly to what many people traditionally consider well decline curves or decline rates.
Will the report include insight into specific technological developments being used in the field?
EIA is tracking industry reports to stay abreast of technological innovation, and the effects of those developments are reflected in the DPR by affecting the average productivity data shown in the report.  However, DPR will not identify the extent to which specific technologies are used in each region or how the application of specific technologies affects the productivity of individual wells.
Will the report include drilling rig availability and economics?
EIA has no current plans to cover these topics in the DPR.
Does the DPR include any classifications or distinctions based on specific operators, subregions, ownership, royalties, or other factors?
The DPR only considers the overall drilling rigs, efficiency metrics, and production levels found within the listed boundaries for each region.
How does the DPR analysis relate to EIA’s oil and natural gas resource assessments?
The DPR looks at active development, not the long-term resource potential within the highlighted regions.  It uses past and present drilling activity to make an estimate of the near-term production that will result directly from that observed activity.
Do production decline rates differ between regions?
Yes.  There are many reasons for the variability in production decline rates, including different geophysical properties of the producing formations, economics, and above-ground takeaway infrastructure.

Operating footprint and responsibilities
A working orientation to Mesa Lantern Energy, its two modeled districts, the functions that own 
records, and the limits of this initial handoff. This draft is prepared for engagement team as part of 
Mesa Lantern Energy's initial information handoff. It describes the modeled operation at the 
stated date and should be read with the period and coverage of its supporting records.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 1
Purpose and immediate use
Use the district and pad view to orient interviews. Field Operations can explain readings and site 
work; Production Accounting owns reviewed volumes; Asset Integrity owns the response to 
equipment findings. The four pads illustrate the scenario footprint rather than exhaustively listing 
every producing site. A location label in an extract should be resolved to the correct district before 
comparing activity.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 2
Operating boundary
Mesa Lantern Energy is modeled as a private onshore operator with two districts: High Plains in 
western Oklahoma and Red Mesa in the Texas Panhandle. Four named pads stand for the field 
footprint in this pilot. The 118 producing wells, roughly 16,400 boe per day, and 74 employees 
describe the modeled business at the reference date; they are planning context, not 
measurements from the supplied extracts.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 3
Decision owners
Field Operations is led by Avery Collins. Robin Vega is accountable for production accounting, 
Morgan Hale for asset integrity, Taylor Kim for development projects, and Casey Nolan for supply 
and contractor records. These assignments identify who can explain a record or approve a 
correction. They do not imply that one person performs every underlying field task or that 
another team may change a source record without its owner.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 4
Daily field-to-ledger path
Field operators enter well readings in Field Log by the next morning. Production Accounting 
compares those entries with Meter Historian readings, records exceptions, and posts reviewed 
values to Production Ledger. A correction preserves the first entry and a reason for the change. 
The review path matters because a later extract should be traceable to the reading and decision 
that produced it.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 5
Work-order route
A field request is tied to an asset and location. The integrity lead prioritizes it, and a supervisor 
confirms isolation and contractor readiness where needed. Completion is not inferred from a 
planned date: closeout requires a completion date, downtime record, and verifier. That sequence 
supports a distinction between an open request, work in progress, and a verified closed order.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 6
Project authorization
Projects and Development separates proposals from authorized work. The meter verification 
campaign is approved and in progress; the Sage Creek pad access improvement remains a 
proposal; the compressor overhaul is approved but has not started. Budget, schedule, owner, and 
approval date belong on milestones. A proposal may be evaluated, but its requested budget or 
target date is not evidence of expenditure or completion.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 7
What the client extract can show
The proposed files are selective extracts from modeled operational registers through August 31, 
2026. Reporting Mart can bring those copies together without changing a source system. The 
package can explain definitions, ownership, and recorded activity within that window. It cannot 
establish complete history, unrecorded field conditions, or companywide production from a 
selected well-day sample.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 8
Record question for review
If a recipient finds a pad label in a workbook but cannot tell which district owns it, first resolve the 
label against the location list. Then ask the named functional owner about the record itself. This 
prevents a production question from being treated as an asset-integrity question merely because 
both concern the same site.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 9
Review action and handoff
The immediate decision is who should answer each follow-up request. Route a measurement 
question to Production Accounting, a closeout question to Asset Integrity, and a proposed capital 
change to Projects and Development. Treat the asset listing as a point-in-time sample and request 
additional history before drawing conclusions about site trends.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Field Operations | 2026-09-26 | 10

files.title: Production review and period close
files.search:
Production review and period close
A period-close briefing on how selected well-day readings become reviewed production entries 
and how later changes are identified. This draft is prepared for operations review group as part of 
Mesa Lantern Energy's initial information handoff. It describes the modeled operation at the 
stated date and should be read with the period and coverage of its supporting records.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 1
Purpose and immediate use
The review should distinguish a field reading, a meter comparison, a posted daily value, and a 
frozen month. Each step has a different status and may appear in a different extract. When a 
correction is discussed, point to its original entry, revised value, date, and reason. Do not put the 
same day into both an original and restated month total.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 2
Daily field-to-ledger path
Field operators enter well readings in Field Log by the next morning. Production Accounting 
compares those entries with Meter Historian readings, records exceptions, and posts reviewed 
values to Production Ledger. A correction preserves the first entry and a reason for the change. 
The review path matters because a later extract should be traceable to the reading and decision 
that produced it.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 3
Production stream definitions
The modeled field ledger holds oil, including lease condensate, in stock tank barrels and raw gas 
in thousand cubic feet at its measurement point. The internal barrel-of-oil-equivalent view uses 
six Mcf of gas for one boe. That ratio is a reporting conversion only; it does not make gas and oil 
economically or energetically identical. Processed natural gas liquids are not attributed to 
individual wells in this extract.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 4
Monthly close boundary
Production Accounting freezes the monthly reporting snapshot on the tenth business day after 
month end. Changes after that point use a dated adjustment record rather than overwriting the 
frozen view. A reader comparing two months must therefore distinguish the original close from a 
later restatement view. The reporting period and extraction date are both necessary to interpret a 
number.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 5
Adjustment lineage
A production adjustment points back to the original daily record, names the stream being 
corrected, and keeps both original and revised values with a posting date and reason. 
Adjustments posted after the monthly freeze belong to a restatement view. Analysts should not 
add both the original and revised quantity when preparing a summary; they should select a 
declared version of the record.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 6
Production measure
For a reviewed well-day, internal boe is oil barrels plus raw gas Mcf divided by six. A month total 
sums the included reviewed daily records; an average daily rate divides by calendar days and must 
be paired with a coverage indicator. Because this pilot extract samples well-days, neither its total 
nor its average can be presented as Mesa Lantern's full operated production without an explicit 
coverage method.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 7
Coverage and missing values
The proposed extracts end on August 31, 2026. Production rows represent selected well-days, 
about 32 of 118 modeled wells per day on average, so their sums are not companywide 
production totals. Some meter or downtime values may be null, with a reason where available. A 
missing value is excluded from a numeric calculation and must never be silently treated as zero.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 8
Record question for review
Take a well-day that has a later adjustment. In the meeting, identify the first reading, the accepted 
entry, the monthly snapshot date, and the adjustment posting date. The exercise shows whether 
two displayed figures are different versions of one observation or genuinely different reporting 
periods.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 9
Review action and handoff
Use any chart only as a view of the selected records. The extract covers a changing subset of 
modeled wells, so its volume line is not a companywide production trend. Ask whether 
differences arise from coverage, revisions, or real changes before using them in a management 
summary.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Production Accounting | 2026-09-26 | 10
Companion extract summary
The accompanying summary is calculated from the selected records in this extract. Read its 
period, contributing-record count, and units before comparing values. It does not substitute for 
the record-level definitions and coverage limitations described above.

files.title: Maintenance and inspection review
files.search:
Maintenance and inspection review
A joint review of work requests, observed conditions, closeout, and the measures used to 
describe the outstanding queue. This draft is prepared for field leadership as part of Mesa Lantern 
Energy's initial information handoff. It describes the modeled operation at the stated date and 
should be read with the period and coverage of its supporting records.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 1
Purpose and immediate use
Follow one equipment concern from an inspection observation to a work request, assignment, 
field readiness, and verified closeout. A late due date does not prove physical work was skipped; it 
does identify a record needing explanation. The inspection register and work register should 
agree on asset, location, and linked order before a combined summary is circulated.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 2
Work-order route
A field request is tied to an asset and location. The integrity lead prioritizes it, and a supervisor 
confirms isolation and contractor readiness where needed. Completion is not inferred from a 
planned date: closeout requires a completion date, downtime record, and verifier. That sequence 
supports a distinction between an open request, work in progress, and a verified closed order.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 3
Maintenance measures
Backlog is the count of open work orders at period end. An overdue order has a due date before 
that point and is not cancelled. Verified downtime hours are summed only where recorded; a 
blank duration is unknown rather than zero. Those definitions prevent an early extract from 
making the outstanding workload or the cost of disruption look smaller than the underlying 
records allow.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 4
Inspection-to-work path
Inspection Register holds scheduled and ad hoc checks of meters, tanks, compressors, and pads. 
An observation may open a linked work order, but the two records answer different questions: the 
inspection records what was seen and the work order records the response. Overdue 
observations stay open until a named owner verifies closure. A scheduled check without a finding 
need not create maintenance work.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 5
Inspection closure measure
The closure rate divides observations closed by observations due in the reporting period. Items 
with future due dates are outside the denominator, even if entered during the period. An analyst 
should preserve open, closed, and not-applicable states separately and inspect linked work orders 
before explaining a change in the rate. The measure describes recorded closeout, not the absence 
of physical defects.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 6
Record linkage
Synthetic well, asset, location, vendor, work-order, and project keys connect the proposed 
datasets. Business users should see natural asset and project names where possible, while the 
keys preserve joins across extracts. A linked inspection and work order should refer to the same 
asset instance and location. A record without a valid link should be flagged for review rather than 
attached to the nearest plausible item.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 7
Coverage and missing values
The proposed extracts end on August 31, 2026. Production rows represent selected well-days, 
about 32 of 118 modeled wells per day on average, so their sums are not companywide 
production totals. Some meter or downtime values may be null, with a reason where available. A 
missing value is excluded from a numeric calculation and must never be silently treated as zero.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 8
Record question for review
Select an observation with a linked work order and check asset instance, location, due date, order 
status, and closure verification. If the observation remains open after the order closes, ask 
whether the integrity owner still needs to verify the result. Do not make the states match by 
editing a report.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 9
Review action and handoff
Discuss backlog and closure rate with their denominators visible. Keep cancelled orders outside 
overdue counts and future-due observations outside the closure-rate denominator. Missing 
downtime remains unknown. The review should result in a list of records to clarify, not an 
invented reliability claim.
Mesa Lantern Energy LLC | Asset Integrity | 2026-09-26 | 10

A paired view of selected well-days and the related adjustment register. This draft is prepared for production review group as part of Mesa Lantern Energy's initial information handoff. It describes the modeled operation at the stated date and should be read with the period and coverage of its supporting records.

Use the separate data tabs to trace an original reading and a revised value. The generic summary of each tab does not reconcile revisions or calculate a company total. Any reviewed series must choose a record version and show sample coverage.

For a reviewed well-day, internal boe is oil barrels plus raw gas Mcf divided by six. A month total sums the included reviewed daily records; an average daily rate divides by calendar days and must be paired with a coverage indicator. Because this pilot extract samples well-days, neither its total nor its average can be presented as Mesa Lantern's full operated production without an explicit coverage method.

The proposed extracts end on August 31, 2026. Production rows represent selected well-days, about 32 of 118 modeled wells per day on average, so their sums are not companywide production totals. Some meter or downtime values may be null, with a reason where available. A missing value is excluded from a numeric calculation and must never be silently treated as zero.

A production adjustment points back to the original daily record, names the stream being corrected, and keeps both original and revised values with a posting date and reason. Adjustments posted after the monthly freeze belong to a restatement view. Analysts should not add both the original and revised quantity when preparing a summary; they should select a declared version of the record.

Start with one adjustment and follow its daily record. Check stream and unit before comparing values. Then decide whether the review calls for the frozen month or a restated view; the workbook's generic per-tab totals cannot answer that choice.
This workbook is for investigating record treatment, not for reporting total field output. Return unresolved links to Production Accounting.

rows: A consolidated field dictionary and small sample index across the selected operational extracts.
See each dataset dictionary and summary. Missing numeric values are excluded, not zero.
Descriptive statistics of selected records only. Totals of percentages and adjustment values are not operating KPIs.

A consolidated field dictionary and small sample index across the selected operational extracts. This draft is prepared for engagement data team as part of Mesa Lantern Energy's initial information handoff. It describes the modeled operation at the stated date and should be read with the period and coverage of its supporting records.

Start with the dictionary tab to understand names, units, types, and source references. Each data tab has its own period and population. Cross-file joins depend on stable keys and should be checked before aggregation.
What the client extract can show

The proposed files are selective extracts from modeled operational registers through August 31, 2026. Reporting Mart can bring those copies together without changing a source system. The package can explain definitions, ownership, and recorded activity within that window. It cannot establish complete history, unrecorded field conditions, or companywide production from a selected well-day sample.

Synthetic well, asset, location, vendor, work-order, and project keys connect the proposed datasets. Business users should see natural asset and project names where possible, while the keys preserve joins across extracts. A linked inspection and work order should refer to the same asset instance and location. A record without a valid link should be flagged for review rather than attached to the nearest plausible item.

The proposed extracts end on August 31, 2026. Production rows represent selected well-days, about 32 of 118 modeled wells per day on average, so their sums are not companywide production totals. Some meter or downtime values may be null, with a reason where available. A missing value is excluded from a numeric calculation and must never be silently treated as zero.

When a new analyst receives the package, ask them to identify the unit, source register, and reporting period for one field in each tab. Any field they cannot explain becomes a dictionary clarification, not an invitation to guess from a similar workbook.
This workbook is an orientation aid. Its combined summary tab is not a cross-domain operating scorecard, and totals from differently scoped files should not be added together.
